title: DID GOD REALLY TELL WOMEN TO BE SILENT IN CHURCH? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING
paragraphs: DID GOD REALLY TELL WOMEN TO BE SILENT IN CHURCH? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING

For centuries, women have been told to sit down, stay quiet, and know their place. Others have been told that Scripture places no boundaries on ministry at all. But what did Jesus actually do? What did Paul really write? And have we sometimes confused God's Word with the traditions we inherited?
Imagine standing in a church where you love Jesus with everything inside you.

You have survived things nobody knows about. You have prayed through nights when sleep wouldn't come. You have carried children, buried dreams, endured betrayal, fought temptation, and held on to God when almost everything else in your life was falling apart.
You know Scripture. You love the Gospel. You want to serve.
And then somebody tells you:
"You're a woman. You need to know your place."
Something inside you goes quiet.
Not because you have stopped loving Jesus.
But because you wonder whether the God who rescued you actually wants to use you.
Now imagine another woman sitting across the same sanctuary.

She has heard people dismiss every biblical distinction between men and women as outdated. She wants to obey Christ, not simply follow culture. Yet whenever she asks what the difficult passages actually mean, someone accuses her of being oppressive or ignorant.
She goes quiet, too.
Two women.
Different convictions.
The same aching question.
Does anyone care enough about the truth to open the Bible without using it as a weapon?
Perhaps you are neither of these women. Perhaps you are a pastor, husband, father, brother, or church leader who sincerely wants to honor God.
Then this question belongs to you, too.
Because how a church treats women reveals something about how seriously it takes the words and example of Jesus Christ.
And there is something astonishing in the Scriptures that we cannot afford to overlook.
When Jesus rose from the dead, the Gospel accounts place women among the first witnesses of the empty tomb and the risen Lord.
Think about that.
At the very heart of Christianity stands the resurrection.
And women were entrusted with the news that changed human history.
But that does not mean every question about church leadership has been settled.
It means we need to listen carefully.
To Jesus.
To the apostles.
To the whole counsel of God.
Because the answer is far richer than the slogans on either side.
And it begins long before anyone ever entered a church building.
In Genesis 1:27, Scripture declares:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — betselem Elohim.
"In the image of God."
Not the man alone.
Not the woman as an afterthought.
Male and female are created in God's image.
This means a woman's worth is not determined by whether she preaches, marries, bears children, leads a ministry, or receives public recognition.
Her dignity was established by her Creator before she accomplished anything.
And so was the man's.
Their shared dignity is not a modern invention.
It is written into creation itself.
Then sin entered the world.
And everything became fractured.

Human beings began turning relationships into struggles for power. Love became entangled with control. Responsibility became an excuse for domination. Differences that could have been expressed through mutual honor became opportunities for pride.
Genesis 3:16 describes the painful disorder that follows the fall, including conflict within the relationship between man and woman.
But describing the consequences of sin is not the same as commanding believers to celebrate those consequences.
Jesus did not come to sanctify human pride.
He came to save sinners and restore people to God.
And when we watch how Jesus treated women, we encounter something extraordinary.
In John 4, Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well.
She arrives carrying a water jar.
But she also carries a complicated history.
Jesus knows about her relationships. He knows the truth she cannot hide. Yet He does not reduce her to the worst or most painful chapters of her life.
He speaks to her about living water.
He reveals Himself to her.
And she leaves her water jar behind.
That detail is almost unbearably beautiful.
The woman who came looking for ordinary water runs toward her community with news of the Messiah.
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" (John 4:29, KJV)
And John tells us that many Samaritans believed because of her testimony.
Do not miss what happened.
A woman with a complicated past became a witness pointing people toward Jesus.
Her history did not become the message.
Christ did.
Her testimony did not replace the Savior.
It led people to Him.
That is what grace does. It does not pretend the past never happened. It gives a redeemed person a future that the past cannot dictate.
Perhaps that is why this story still reaches people who have spent years feeling disqualified.
The divorced woman who wonders whether God can still use her.
The single mother who feels invisible.
The widow whose voice has been overlooked.
The young woman who wants to study Scripture but has been told that serious theology is not for her.
The woman who has repented of terrible decisions and still wonders whether the church will ever see anything beyond her past.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not promise everyone the same ministry assignment.
But He does call sinners to Himself, forgive those who repent, and make His people fruitful in His service.
Your past does not outrank His grace.
And your gender does not cancel your identity as someone made in God's image.
Consider Mary of Bethany.
In Luke 10:38–42, while Martha is occupied with serving, Mary sits at Jesus' feet and listens to His teaching.
That expression matters.
Mary is not merely present in the room.
She is receiving instruction from the Master.
Jesus says she has chosen the good portion.
He does not rebuke her for wanting to learn.
He defends her opportunity to hear His Word.
And here is a question every church should be willing to face:
If Jesus welcomed Mary as a serious learner of divine truth, why would we discourage women from studying theology, understanding doctrine, asking difficult questions, and growing in biblical wisdom?
A church that wants faithful women must be willing to teach women faithfully.
Not merely entertain them.
Not merely give them tasks.
Teach them the Scriptures.
Help them recognize false doctrine.
Equip them to disciple others.
Because biblical ignorance does not become holiness simply because it is quiet.
Then we arrive at the resurrection.
In John 20, Mary Magdalene stands outside the tomb, weeping.
She believes she has lost the One who changed her life.
And then Jesus speaks her name.
"Mary."
One word.
And grief begins to give way to recognition.
The woman who had been crying outside a grave is now encountering the risen Christ.
Jesus instructs her to go to His brethren with His message.
And John 20:18 records:
"Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her." (KJV)
She did not invent the message.
She did not appoint herself Savior.
She bore witness to what Christ had revealed.
The resurrection announcement was not a human reward for being important.
It was news entrusted by the risen Lord.
And that distinction matters.
Mary's testimony does not automatically establish that women should occupy every ordained office.
But neither can anyone honestly use the Bible to argue that women have no meaningful responsibility to speak of Christ.
Jesus Himself sent Mary with news of His resurrection.
How could the church possibly conclude that women's voices are spiritually irrelevant?
Yet we must keep reading.
Because Scripture does not stop with the Gospels.
In Acts 2, the Holy Spirit is poured out at Pentecost.
Peter explains the event by quoting the prophet Joel.
"And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy." (Acts 2:18, KJV)
The Greek expression αἱ δοῦλαί μου — hai doulai mou refers to "my female servants."
The promise explicitly includes women.
Not as spectators outside the work of God.
As recipients of the Spirit's outpouring.
And the passage speaks of prophecy.
This does not mean every believer receives the same gift, nor does it settle every question about the relationship between prophecy, teaching, and church office.
But it establishes something that should never be controversial.
The Holy Spirit does not treat women as second-class members of Christ's body.
Paul makes another remarkable declaration in Galatians 3:28:
"There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." (KJV)
The Greek concludes:
πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς εἷς ἐστε ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — pantes gar hymeis heis este en Christō Iēsou.
"For you are all one in Christ Jesus."
Paul is speaking about belonging to Christ and sharing in the inheritance promised through Him.
He is not saying biological differences disappear or that every role in the church becomes identical.
But he is absolutely declaring that men and women do not enter the family of God through different doors.
There is one Savior.
One Gospel.
One salvation.
One inheritance in Christ.
A woman is not spiritually inferior to a man.
A man is not spiritually superior because he is male.
Both must come to the same cross.
Both must repent.
Both must be saved by grace.
And both must submit to the Lordship of Jesus.
So why does Paul sometimes appear to tell women to remain silent?
This is where many conversations become heated.
And where careful Bible reading becomes especially important.
First Corinthians 14:34 says:
"Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak..." (KJV)
Read that sentence alone, and it can sound like an absolute prohibition against any woman speaking during a Christian gathering.
But only three chapters earlier, in 1 Corinthians 11:5, Paul refers to a woman praying or prophesying.
Whatever disagreements Christians have about the conditions and setting of those activities, Paul clearly acknowledges women praying and prophesying.
Therefore, we must ask whether the silence commanded in chapter 14 concerns every form of speech or a particular kind of speaking within the worship gathering.
The surrounding chapter addresses orderly worship, the evaluation of prophecy, and avoiding confusion.
Paul also commands certain tongue-speakers to keep silent when no interpreter is present, and prophets to become silent when another receives a revelation.
The Greek verb σιγάω — sigaō means to be silent or keep quiet.
Its meaning must be understood within each instruction's context.

Many interpreters therefore understand the restriction on women in 1 Corinthians 14 as addressing disruptive speech, certain forms of questioning, or the authoritative evaluation of prophecy rather than forbidding every spoken contribution by women.
Others understand the passage as establishing a broader restriction related to authority in gathered worship.
These interpretations are debated among Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture.
We should not pretend the debate disappears simply because one explanation feels more comfortable.
And we should not accuse every believer who disagrees with our interpretation of hating women or rejecting the Bible.
But another passage demands our attention.
First Timothy 2:12.
"But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence." (KJV)
Here we need to be especially careful.
The Greek includes:
διδάσκειν — didaskein, meaning "to teach."
And:
αὐθεντεῖν — authentein, a comparatively rare verb whose precise nuance is debated, commonly translated in this context as "to exercise authority."

The older English phrase "usurp authority" can suggest taking authority improperly. But the Greek word itself does not conclusively establish that Paul was prohibiting only abusive or domineering authority.
Some scholars argue for a negative nuance. Others argue that the ordinary exercise of authority is in view.
The immediate context and Paul's appeal to Adam and Eve in verses 13–14 are important parts of the discussion.

Christians who hold the complementarian position generally understand this passage, alongside 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1, as reserving the governing and authoritative teaching office of elder or pastor to qualified men.
They emphasize that equal dignity does not require identical responsibilities.

Christians who hold the egalitarian position generally understand the restrictions in light of the specific circumstances facing Timothy's congregation and the broader biblical witness to women's ministry. They conclude that qualified women may also serve in pastoral leadership.
Both positions contain serious arguments that deserve careful engagement.
Neither should be caricatured.
The complementarian must explain why the many women commended for ministry in Scripture matter and how restrictions should be applied without diminishing their gifts.
The egalitarian must explain Paul's explicit instructions and his appeal to creation rather than treating difficult verses as disposable.
And both must answer to the same Lord.
Because the question is not merely, "Which interpretation gives me the outcome I prefer?"
The question is, "What did God communicate through His Word, and how do we obey Him faithfully?"
That requires more than quoting a single verse.
It requires studying the whole passage, understanding the historical setting, examining the original language, and allowing Scripture to interpret Scripture.
It also requires humility.
No amount of Greek vocabulary can make a disputed interpretation automatically certain.
And no amount of emotional passion can make an argument biblical if it contradicts the text.
We must love the truth more than winning.
Now consider the women who served alongside the apostles.
Romans 16 introduces us to Phoebe.
Paul writes:
The Greek describes her as a διάκονον — diakonon of the church.
The word can mean servant, minister, or deacon, depending on its context.
Some understand Phoebe as holding a recognized diaconal office. Others understand Paul as commending her significant service without necessarily assigning a formal office.
Paul also calls her a helper of many, including himself.
The Greek term προστάτις — prostatis can carry the sense of patron, protector, or benefactor.
Phoebe was not insignificant.
Paul publicly commended her.
Then there is Priscilla.
Acts 18 tells us that Priscilla and Aquila encountered Apollos, an eloquent man who was knowledgeable in Scripture but needed a fuller understanding of the way of God.
They took him aside and explained that way more accurately.
Notice what the text actually says.
Priscilla and Aquila participated together in helping a gifted man understand Christian truth more fully.
The passage does not explicitly identify Priscilla as a congregational elder or describe a formal sermon.
But it certainly does not portray her as incapable of explaining doctrine.
Aquila was not diminished because his wife understood the Scriptures.
Apollos was not diminished because he received correction from a married couple that included a woman.
Truth mattered more than wounded pride.
And perhaps that is a lesson many churches desperately need.
In Romans 16:7, Paul also greets Andronicus and Junia.
The Greek name Ἰουνίαν — Iounian is widely understood by contemporary scholars as referring to a woman named Junia.
Paul describes the pair with an expression commonly translated "outstanding among the apostles," although some interpret it as "well known to the apostles."
Even the meaning of "apostles" in this context is discussed.
We should neither erase Junia's significance nor claim that one debated phrase settles every question about pastoral office.
What cannot be ignored is that Paul honors women as meaningful participants in the work of the Gospel.
And he does not stop there.
He commends Mary for her labor.
He greets Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord.
He honors Persis, who worked hard in the Lord.
These women were not decorative additions to the early church.
Their work mattered.
Their faithfulness mattered.
Their service was remembered.
And God inspired Paul to include their names in Scripture.
Think about that for a moment.
Some people have spent centuries arguing over whether women matter in ministry.
Meanwhile, the Bible itself preserves the names of women whose labor helped strengthen the church.
There is a difference between honoring biblical distinctions and treating women as though their only contribution is to remain unnoticed.
The first may arise from sincere convictions about Scripture.
The second contradicts the example of the apostles.
And we must also remember the women who served God long before the New Testament.
Deborah judged Israel and spoke as a prophetess (Judges 4–5).
Huldah was a prophetess consulted during the reign of Josiah (2 Kings 22).
Miriam was called a prophetess (Exodus 15:20).
Their responsibilities arose in particular historical and covenantal settings. We should not simply equate those roles with the office of New Testament elder.
But neither should we act as though God has never entrusted women with weighty spiritual responsibilities.
He has.
The Bible says so.
And there is another passage that may be especially important for the church today.
Titus 2:3–5 instructs older women to live reverently and teach what is good, training younger women in godly living.
This is not a minor assignment.
Imagine the spiritual damage that could be prevented if mature Christian women were intentionally equipped to disciple younger women.
Imagine the marriages strengthened.
The children nurtured.
The wounded encouraged.
The confused taught.
The lonely welcomed.
The grieving comforted.
The new believers grounded in Scripture.
The women trapped in shame reminded of the forgiveness available through Christ.
Imagine what would happen if churches stopped measuring spiritual significance solely by who stands behind the pulpit.
Because not every calling requires a microphone.
And not every quiet act of faithfulness is small.
A woman opening her Bible with a younger believer may be participating in work whose eternal fruit she will never fully see.
A mother teaching her child to pray is doing something spiritually significant.
A single woman discipling others is not waiting for marriage before her life becomes useful to God.
A widow encouraging the church through steadfast faith is not finished serving because one season of life has ended.

A woman who supports missions, cares for the suffering, evangelizes, teaches in appropriate settings, organizes mercy ministries, or uses her gifts faithfully is not a lesser Christian because her ministry is not public.
And a man who serves quietly is not lesser either.
In the kingdom of God, visibility is not the measure of faithfulness.
Jesus said:
"But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant." (Matthew 23:11, KJV)
The Greek word for servant in this verse is διάκονος — diakonos.
One who serves.
It is a word that should humble every Christian who wants authority more than responsibility.
And this brings us to a painful reality.
Sometimes, churches have used passages about submission to protect the wrong people.
A woman raises concerns about manipulation, abuse, or serious misconduct.
Someone tells her to be quiet.
A wife asks for help because she is being harmed.
Someone tells her that submission means enduring whatever happens.
A young woman asks a sincere biblical question.
Someone treats her curiosity as rebellion.
That is not a faithful application of Scripture.
Biblical submission never gives anyone permission to sin, abuse, intimidate, or conceal wrongdoing.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
That is sacrificial love.
Not exploitation.
Not coercion.
Not the protection of a man's reputation at the expense of a woman's safety.
Jesus did not teach leaders to lord their authority over others.
He taught them to serve.
A church that takes Scripture seriously must also take justice, truthfulness, protection of the vulnerable, and accountability seriously.
Women should be able to report abuse and seek safety without being accused of disobeying God.
And the church should never confuse silencing a victim with preserving unity.
Unity built on concealed evil is not the holiness Christ commands.
But we must speak another truth just as clearly.
Some churches, reacting against genuine mistreatment, may become tempted to dismiss every biblical instruction about order, authority, and qualifications for ministry.
That is not the answer either.
We cannot correct the misuse of Scripture by refusing to submit to Scripture.
We cannot defeat pride by replacing it with another form of pride.
We cannot honor women by teaching them that faithfulness means ignoring passages they find difficult.
Christ calls every disciple to obedience.
Male and female.
Leader and member.
Teacher and learner.
All of us.
And this is where the conversation must become deeply personal.
Because beneath the argument about women in ministry lies a question that confronts every human heart.
Do I want Jesus to be Lord, or do I only want Him to approve what I already believe?
That question can expose all of us.
The man who loves authority but avoids accountability.
The woman who longs for recognition more than service.
The pastor who refuses to examine a cherished tradition.
The Christian who dismisses a difficult passage without studying it.
The believer who confuses a cultural preference with an eternal command.
The person who has been wounded so deeply that trusting any spiritual leader feels impossible.
We all need the mercy of Christ.
And we all need the transforming power of His Word.
The church does not belong to men.
It does not belong to women.
It belongs to Jesus.
He purchased it with His blood.
He is its Head.
And every ministry within it must be accountable to Him.
So what is the role of women in churches today?
Women are called, like men, to be disciples of Jesus Christ.
To repent and believe the Gospel.
To worship God.
To study and obey Scripture.
To pray.
To bear witness to Christ.
To exercise the spiritual gifts God has entrusted to them in ways consistent with biblical teaching.
To make disciples.
To encourage the suffering.
To confront sin appropriately.
To practice mercy.
To teach and mentor in biblically faithful settings.
To support the church's mission.
To pursue holiness.
To serve as indispensable members of Christ's body.

Regarding the specific office of elder or pastor and the exercise of authoritative teaching in gathered worship, faithful Christians continue to disagree about the proper interpretation of the relevant passages.
Churches should examine those texts carefully, state their convictions honestly, and apply them consistently without degrading those who hold a different interpretation.

And regardless of which position a church adopts, no congregation should treat women as spiritually inferior, deny them serious biblical education, or neglect the gifts and service Scripture clearly recognizes.
First Corinthians 12 teaches that the church is one body with many members.
The body cannot function properly when its members despise one another.
And no Christian should confuse having a particular assignment with having greater worth before God.
We have spent so much time asking who gets the highest position.
Perhaps we should also ask who is willing to wash the feet.
Who will visit the sick?
Who will disciple the teenager wrestling with doubt?
Who will sit beside the woman who has just lost her husband?
Who will tell the young mother that her exhaustion has not made her invisible to God?
Who will explain the Gospel patiently to someone who has never understood grace?
Who will lovingly confront false teaching?
Who will pray when nobody is watching?
Who will serve when there is no applause?
Because one day, the applause of people will mean nothing.
And the approval of Christ will mean everything.
Perhaps the most heartbreaking tragedy is not that some women have been denied a platform.
It is that some have been made to feel that God has no purpose for them unless they have one.
And perhaps another tragedy is that some have been taught to measure their value by obtaining the very authority Jesus taught His followers not to idolize.
The Gospel frees us from both lies.
You do not need to become famous to be faithful.
You do not need to control others to be significant.
You do not need a title to be loved by God.
You need Christ.
And when you belong to Him, your life becomes an offering of worship.
Romans 12:1 calls believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
That calling belongs to the whole church.
It is not divided into first-class and second-class Christians.
Now think again about the woman at the well.
She arrived with a complicated story.
She encountered Jesus.
She returned to her community with a testimony.
And people came to hear Him.
The story did not end with people admiring her.
It ended with people recognizing the Savior.
John 4:42 records their confession:
"...we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world." (KJV)
There it is.
The true goal of Christian ministry.
Not that people become dependent on our personalities.
Not that they celebrate our influence.
Not that they remember our names above the name of Jesus.
But that they come to know Him.
And perhaps this is the truth that every Christian, whether male or female, needs to hear today.
Your greatest calling is not to prove how important you are in the church. It is to make Christ known through a life surrendered to Him.
For the woman who has been silenced unjustly, may you find healing, wise counsel, and a church that honors both Scripture and your God-given dignity.
For the woman who has been entrusted with significant ministry responsibility, may you serve with humility, courage, sound doctrine, and accountability.
For the woman whose ministry happens in kitchens, hospital rooms, classrooms, homes, and unnoticed places, may you never confuse being unseen by people with being unseen by God.
For the man who has used biblical language to justify pride, may repentance lead you toward the servant-hearted example of Jesus.
For the church leader who is genuinely trying to understand these difficult passages, may you have the courage to follow Scripture even when the answer challenges your assumptions.
And for every believer caught in the middle of this debate, may we remember that our deepest unity is not found in winning an argument.
It is found in the crucified and risen Lord.
The same Jesus who spoke to Mary at the tomb.
The same Jesus who welcomed Mary of Bethany as a learner.
The same Jesus who revealed Himself to the Samaritan woman.
The same Jesus who died for our sins and rose again.
He is still calling people out of darkness.
Still forgiving the repentant.
Still restoring the broken.
Still transforming sinners into servants.
Still building His church.
And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Before you leave this article, I want to ask you something that cannot be answered by winning a theological debate.
Have you ever felt overlooked, dismissed, or unworthy of being used by God?
Or have you ever realized that your own pride made someone else feel that way?
Be honest.
Because the answer might reveal where Jesus is calling you to repent, heal, forgive, or grow.
And if you have seen Christ work through the faithfulness of a woman in your life, tell us about it.
Maybe it was your mother.
Your grandmother.
A Sunday school teacher.
A missionary.
A woman who discipled you.
Someone who prayed for you when you had nearly given up.
Let her faithfulness be remembered.
Your testimony may encourage someone who has begun to believe that her service does not matter.
Not to provoke another exhausting argument.
But to invite people into a conversation where biblical truth matters more than personal attacks.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter daily Scripture, Gospel-centered conviction, encouragement, repentance, forgiveness, healing, and serious discipleship.
And if these messages have strengthened your faith, there is another way you can help us continue.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
We want more people to have access to biblical teaching.
More families to discover Christ-centered resources.
More struggling believers to find encouragement rooted in Scripture.
More people to hear that forgiveness and new life are found in Jesus.
But producing, organizing, and expanding ministry resources requires time, work, and practical support.
It does not purchase a blessing.
It does not make you a more valuable Christian.
And it should never replace the giving responsibilities you prayerfully discern toward your local church and those in need.
Rather, it is a voluntary way to support Gospel-centered work beyond your local congregation.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
Because ministry support should flow from love, not guilt.
These products are simply resources and reminders. They are not the reason we preach the Gospel.
Jesus is.
If you are able and willing to support, we would be grateful to have you walking alongside us.
Read the Scriptures.
Share the Gospel.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
There are many ways to participate in the work of making Christ known.
And none of them should be confused with purchasing a place in God's family.
That place is received through faith in Jesus Christ, by grace.
Now, before this article ends, return with me to that garden outside the empty tomb.
Mary is crying.
Her heart is shattered.
She believes the story is over.
Then the risen Savior calls her name.
And everything changes.
She came expecting to mourn the dead.
She left bearing witness to the living Christ.
That is the beauty of redemption.
Jesus takes people who have been broken by sin, sorrow, shame, and suffering and gives them a new life in Him.
He does not promise that every Christian will have the same role.
He promises something infinitely greater to those who belong to Him.
His presence.
His forgiveness.
His resurrection life.
And the privilege of serving His purposes.
So whether you are a woman who has been overlooked, a man learning to lead with humility, or a believer trying to understand the Bible faithfully, remember this:
The church was never meant to be a battlefield where we compete for human importance.
It is meant to be a redeemed people who bow before one Lord.
And when the church truly understands that, women will not need to be diminished for men to be honored.
Men will not need to be diminished for women to be valued.
And neither will need to compete for the glory that belongs to Jesus alone.
Because the cross has already settled the question of how much we are worth to the Savior who gave Himself for us.
And the empty tomb has already declared who deserves the highest place.
The woman at the tomb did not have to become the center of the story to carry the greatest news the world had ever heard: Jesus was alive.
